title: WHY HAILSTONES HAVE LAYERS LIKE AN ONION
display: about a hundred and fifteen kilometers per hour

segments.heading: 10 CM OF ICE
segments.text: Slice a big hailstone in half: layers, like an onion.
segments.event: NSSL: layers of clear and cloudy ice.

segments.heading: THE OLD STORY
segments.text: The classic story: each layer is one more trip up and down the storm.

segments.heading: THE TWIST
segments.text: But storm scientists say that's not the whole story.

segments.heading: CLOUDY ICE
segments.text: When water freezes on the stone instantly, it traps air bubbles. That makes cloudy ice.

segments.heading: CLEAR ICE
segments.text: When it freezes slowly, the bubbles escape. That makes clear ice.

segments.heading: A MAP OF THE STORM
segments.text: The layers record changing conditions as the stone drifts sideways near the updraft.

segments.heading: NOT AT THE TOP
segments.text: And it doesn't grow at the storm's top. Up there it's below minus forty degrees, and all the water is frozen.
segments.event: NSSL: below −40 °F all liquid water frozen (−40 °F = −40 °C).

segments.heading: FALL SPEED
segments.text: Stones this size can hit about a hundred and fifteen kilometers per hour.
